question: Does relational structure have the SECOND holographic property — distributedness? Does every fragment carry information about the whole, or does information sit in specific places?
why_this_is_the_on-thesis_test: Lee's restatement: the thesis is that nothing exists in a vacuum and everything leaves an imprint on everything else, with holography as the model — light's interference records relationships that intensity recording discards. We have verified the FIRST holographic property (C-01: structure exists that no pairwise view contains, i.e. interference carries what intensity does not). The SECOND property is distributedness: cut a hologram in half and you get the whole scene at reduced resolution, not half a scene. Nobody has tested whether relational structure behaves that way, and it is the sharper of the two claims.

the_analogy_made_precise.intensity recording: measure each thing's own properties — single-variable influences
the_analogy_made_precise.interference recording: measure the relations — the subset-indexed invariant, all orders
the_analogy_made_precise.a fragment of the plate: a random subset of those measurements
the_analogy_made_precise.the holographic claim: a fragment of the interference record still describes the WHOLE object, degrading in resolution rather than in coverage. A fragment of an intensity record describes only the part it covers.

design: Exhaustive over Boolean systems of 4 variables where the complete invariant is known. Take a fraction f of the available measurements, and ask how many distinct systems that fragment can still tell apart. Two conditions: RELATIONAL fragments (drawn from the subset-indexed invariant at all orders) and PROPERTY fragments (drawn from single-variable terms only). Sweep f.
statistic: discrimination retained = (distinct equivalence classes under the fragment) / (distinct classes under the full invariant), per fraction f
tests: descriptive curves over f, averaged across many random fragments per f. No null-hypothesis test: the shape of the curve is the answer.
exclusion_rule: systems whose full invariant is degenerate (all-zero) are excluded and counted — they are indistinguishable from each other under any fragment and would flatter both arms equally.
robustness: report the whole curve, not a point. Report the property arm's ceiling explicitly, since a hard ceiling is the signature the analogy predicts.
falsification: relational fragments degrade at the SAME rate as property fragments -> relational structure is not distributed, the holographic analogy fails at its second property, and the thesis loses its sharper half
relational fragments degrade GRACEFULLY while property fragments hit a hard ceiling -> the analogy holds on this class of systems
both hit ceilings -> neither is distributed and the analogy is decorative

predictions.claim: property fragments will hit a hard ceiling well below 1.0
predictions.reason: single-variable influences are a lossy summary by C-06 — two systems can agree on every influence and still differ. The ceiling is the size of that collision set

predictions.claim: relational fragments will degrade gracefully and approach 1.0
predictions.reason: this is the thesis's own claim and I am therefore inclined to believe it, which is the reason to be careful. It could equally be that discrimination sits concentrated in the high-order terms, in which case a random fragment usually misses them and degrades sharply

predictions.claim: if prediction 2 fails, that is the most important negative the project could produce — it would mean the holographic analogy is decorative rather than structural
predictions.confidence: n/a — stated so it cannot be softened later
